title: Stoke Space’s Nova Pathfinder booster arrives at SLC-14 ahead of 2027 debut - NASASpaceFlight.com
html:
Stoke Space’s Nova Pathfinder is moving toward an early 2027 inaugural launch following the arrival of its first stage at Space Launch Complex 14 (SLC-14) at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 22.

Following a 17-day cross-country road trip from Washington, the booster has entered SLC-14’s Horizontal Integration Facility (HIF) ahead of a pad-in-the-loop wet dress rehearsal campaign.

The campaign will also activate the newly rebuilt complex, marking the first time a rocket has occupied the historic pad since the 1960s.

Meanwhile, Stoke is preparing to conduct a Stage 2 static fire at its Moses Lake Test Site (MLTS) in December, once engineers mate the upper stage with its Andromeda engine.

There’s a rocket at SLC-14 for the first time in 60 years.

Nova Pathfinder’s first stage rolled into Cape Canaveral on Sunday ahead of our first orbital launch.

Read about the test campaign that got us here and what’s next before we fly. ⬇️ https://t.co/1O2sw6cVkU pic.twitter.com/cbNU8TDAX9

— Stoke Space (@stoke_space) November 24, 2026

Stage 1 and Zenith Propulsion

With the arrival of Stage 1 at SLC-14, Stoke is preparing to conduct a series of tests.

The first stage will undergo wet dress rehearsals (WDRs) that will fill the vehicle with cryogenic propellants and test the launch infrastructure, including the tank farms.

Once Stage 1 has completed its WDRs, the vehicle will roll back to the HIF to have its remaining Zenith engines integrated.

After engine installation, the stage will return to the pad to conduct a static fire before rolling back to the HIF to eventually mate with its second stage.

Getting to this point required months of structural testing and qualification. In May, the flight stage undertook its proto-qualification campaign at MLTS.

During the three-week campaign, the structure completed 46 structural test objectives, and engineers loaded it to 115% of expected flight loads. Stoke used hundreds of strain gauges to verify the vehicle behaved as predicted.

The structural qualification began long before this, however, with Stoke testing “dogbone” material coupons to quantify strength before and after each manufacturing step.

By subjecting these samples to heated and cryogenic testing, engineers verified the integrity of welds and fabrication processes across representative flight temperatures. That data was then used to build the test matrix for larger structural articles.

After this initial testing, Stoke moved on to “Tiny Tank” ground test articles. The Tiny Tanks were full-diameter, shortened versions of the flight tanks, used to push the structure past expected flight loads and identify any design issues.

“Tiny Tank 1” was pushed to failure and burst in 2025, while “Tiny Tank 2” stayed within its design margins and was used to qualify the Stage 1 aft barrels.

Zenith engines (Credit: Stoke Space)

Alongside the structural campaign, Stoke has been qualifying and accepting the seven full-flow staged combustion Zenith engines that will power Pathfinder’s first stage.

Four of the seven flight engines have completed acceptance testing, with the remaining three actively moving through testing ahead of shipment to Florida.

Over a two-year development period, Zenith progressed through four different block configurations before the design was locked for qualification and acceptance testing. These changes covered areas such as turbopumps, valves, the thrust chamber, and other components.

Stoke also brought seal production in-house, and the first in-house produced seal was installed on an engine within three weeks of the decision.

Following the design lock, Stoke conducted nearly 10,000 seconds of hot-fire testing over five months to qualify Zenith for flight.

Two dedicated qualification engines accumulated 7,647 seconds across 91 starts, demonstrating approximately ten times the engine’s initial service-life requirement of 760 seconds.

Stage 2 and Andromeda

Pathfinder’s second stage arrived at the MLTS in late October for structural qualification and was vertical on its test stand within 24 hours of arrival.

By the beginning of November, the stage had completed its structural proof testing with cryogenic propellants. This included the oxidizer tank, common dome, and fuel tank, which were each taken to 110% of the stage’s design pressure.

Stoke held these structures for five minutes and observed no structural anomalies after the process.

Once the stage had completed the proof testing, it conducted a full WDR with its liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen (hydrolox) propellants. The test successfully rehearsed the full launch sequence, and the vehicle was filled to its flight loads.

Comparison Zenith and Andromeda hot fire tests (Credit: Stoke Space)

At the base of the upper stage sits Andromeda, the most novel element of Nova’s architecture.

Rather than relying on ablative materials or ceramic tiles for atmospheric reentry, Andromeda integrates a hydrolox propulsion system directly into an actively cooled, ductile metallic heat shield.

By circulating cryogenic propellant through the shield during entry, the stage is designed to endure repeated thermal cycles with minimal inspection or refurbishment between flights.

Stoke first fired a 30-thruster development version of Andromeda in February 2024. Since then, the program has progressed through 50 hardware configurations and 242 total starts.

The last 15 months alone accounted for three engines, 30 hardware configurations, 72 starts, and 10,825 seconds of hot-fire time. The qualification campaign included 28 starts and 5,177 seconds, reaching twice the engine’s rated flight life.

With tank proof testing and WDRs complete, Stage 2 is ready for its December static fire once mated with its accepted Andromeda engine.

Stage 2 at the Moses Lake Test Site (Credit: Stoke Space)

Nova Block 2

Looking beyond Pathfinder’s first launch, the flight will serve as a direct proving ground for Nova Block 2, a heavy-lift variant Stoke unveiled in September alongside a $1 billion Series E raise.

Targeted for a first flight in 2029, Block 2 scales up Pathfinder’s core architecture by doubling the booster to 14 Zenith engines. The upper stage moves to a 24-thruster Andromeda configuration with a five-meter fairing.

Block 2 is designed to lift 15 metric tons to low Earth orbit in a fully reusable configuration.

It will operate alongside Pathfinder to support high-cadence commercial constellation deployments, including a recently signed multi-launch agreement with Planet Labs.

Besides the company’s pad at SLC-14, Space Launch Delta 45 granted Stoke Right of Entry (RoE) to expand into the area north of the existing pad.

From there, the company will be able to conduct engineering studies, site surveys, and environmental assessments with a view to building a second pad for Nova on the site.
